name: Effect
desc: Plays a sound effect or particle effect at a position (without a named sound).

fields.name: disableRelativeVolume
fields.desc: If true, plays at full volume regardless of position

notes: Effect IDs: 1000-1023 (sound events), 1500-2004 (particle events). Unlike S29 (named sound via resource location), S28 uses numeric IDs.

writeup.p: S28 is the numeric sound/particle effect packet: an int effect type, a BlockPos, an int data value, and a boolean that forces server-wide volume. Effect IDs are split into ranges: 1000-1023 for sound events (anvil, click, door) and 1500-2004 for particle/block events (smoke, portal, beacon, chest open particle). WorldManager sends it either to players near the position (64-block radius, volume-attenuated) or to every player when the server-wide flag is set (corpus lines 82/86).

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEffect branches on the server-wide flag: isSoundServerwide routes to world.func_175669_a (global sound), otherwise world.playAuxSFX(type, pos, data), which maps the numeric ID to a sound or particle burst and plays it with position-based volume. The data int is effect-specific (block ID for break particles, pitch for sounds). There is no client feedback path; the packet is fire-and-forget.

Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's script NetworkAPI registration. The packet metadata mentions ESP tracking record players and particles, but no module in these 8 clients implements it. The reason is redundancy: effect sounds and particles are transient and position-derived, and anything a module could learn (a chest opening nearby, a beacon activating) is already visible through block state or S24.

The exploitable direction is server to client: a malicious server can spam S28 with high-volume sound IDs or particle-heavy IDs to annoy or degrade the client (the classic record-spam or smoke-spam lag nuisance). The client applies each effect without rate limiting, which is why crash-patch modules bound effect rates. No corpus module does this for S28; Tenacity's AntiExploit covers the particle flood via S2APacketParticles instead, which is the named-particle equivalent.

implementation.overview: The numeric sound/particle effect packet with a server-wide volume flag. Zero modules in the 8 clients consume it; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's scripting API registration. Transient, position-derived and fire-and-forget, it carries nothing a module needs that block state does not already provide.
implementation.server_handling: WorldManager.func_180439_a sends S28 to players within 64 blocks with serverWide=false; func_180440_b sends it to all players with serverWide=true (used for dimension-wide events like beacon activation or the wither spawn). The server never validates the effect ID or data against a whitelist, so any int in range goes through. No rate limit in vanilla.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: int effect type, BlockPos long, int data, boolean serverWide. The effect type is a raw int, unlike S29PacketSoundEffect which carries a resource location; this is the 'numeric' counterpart. The boolean is a plain byte on the wire (writeBoolean/readBoolean). The data int is interpreted per effect ID, so the same int means block ID for break particles and pitch for sounds.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not monitored. Effects carry no player state, and the only abuse is nuisance flooding, which anti-cheats handle by rate-limiting inbound effect packets rather than flagging players. Client-side crash patches treat S28 and S2A as the same threat class (audio/particle floods), but none of the 8 clients ships that guard for S28 specifically.
implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is available on all clients; no module registers for S28 in the corpus.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients keep the vanilla handler. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 register S28 in the script NetworkAPI table only. Tenacity's AntiExploit limits the S2APacketParticles flood but not the numeric S28 path.
